cells.tense: You're watching something come apart and you can name why it had to.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's ending and put a sentence down about what it actually was. Plain words, one line. Then leave it — no plan, no next step, just the line.
cells.core:
You can stand inside something ending and still read why it had to. What held it together, what wore through first, why the shape it had couldn't carry the weight any more. That reading isn't a way of skipping the loss — it's the thing keeping you upright while the loss happens.

This is the balance: clarity and hurt in the same room, neither one cancelling the other. You're not narrating from a distance. You're in it, and you can still see. What you notice is worth keeping — not as a lesson, just as a record. In a year it'll say more to you than the feeling did.
cells.sheetLine: You can watch it end and still see it clearly.
cells.verb: seeing the mechanism under what's falling away
cells.place: at an ending that hasn't finished happening

cells.tense: You're reading the shape of endings that haven't happened yet.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've decided is ending. Say it in a single sentence and stop — no reasons, no timing, no next move. If you can't, that's the answer for today.
cells.core:
A friendship twigged something and you've already mapped how it runs out. A job goes slightly sideways and you can see the exit. The reading is fast and mostly right, and it's become constant rehearsal for losses that may not arrive.

What it costs is the thing in front of you. You're not in the friendship — you're in the ending of it. The other person feels the distance, and the distance is doing more damage than anything you spotted would have.

There's a real signal. But reading a shape and grieving it ahead of time aren't the same job, and the rehearsal isn't sparing you anything that's coming.
cells.sheetLine: You're already grieving an ending that hasn't started.
cells.verb: seeing the mechanism under what's falling away
cells.place: at an ending that hasn't finished happening

cells.tense: Something ended and you've been calling it bad timing.
cells.ask: Write one plain sentence about what ended — what it was, not why. Read it once, then put it away. Don't turn it into a lesson yet.
cells.core:
A way of working, a closeness, a version of yourself — it finished, and you've kept the description flat. Bad luck. Wrong moment. Things changed. Nothing worth looking at. Staying in the literal keeps it manageable, and that got you through; you're still going.

What this looks like when it's working is simple enough: you can say what a thing was without dressing it up or cutting it down. Just the plain account, held long enough to be true. That's what's missing here.

The flatness is costing you. Whatever formed that ending is still operating, and you can't spot it, so you'll meet it again in the next thing without recognising it. One honest sentence about what was there is enough to start. You don't need the story.
cells.sheetLine: What ended had a shape. You've been calling it timing.
cells.verb: seeing the mechanism under what's falling away

cells.tense: An arrangement finished and you're still describing it as ongoing.
cells.ask: Say to someone close, in your own words, that you think something has ended. One sentence, no explanation. Notice what it's like to have said it out loud.
cells.core:
A working relationship quietly stopped being one. A closeness thinned out months ago. A self you used to be hasn't shown up in a while. You know each of these things, and you're still filing them under normal.

When this capacity is running clean, someone can tell you what ended and what came after in one breath, without flinching or making it into a story. You can do that too — but not while half the arrangement is still described in present tense.

Saying it would mean standing somewhere. Turning down the invitations you keep half-accepting. Speaking plainly to the person you've been careful around. The pattern is already running the situation. The sentence isn't the ending. It's the first honest thing you'd say about it.
cells.sheetLine: It already ended. You're still talking about it in present tense.
cells.verb: seeing the mechanism under what's falling away
cells.place: at an ending that hasn't finished happening
